facts.F1: There are three categories of overseas officers: (1) those who started their LMT agreements during the freeze, (2) those who began their LMT agreements before the freeze and can choose any date between the start date and the expiry of their current agreements, and (3) those whose 50th birthday occurred before they became LMT officers.
facts.F2: The Circular of 1993 froze the transfer of overseas officers to pensionable terms, and this decision was declared unlawful by Keith J in 1995.
facts.F3: The freeze was a consequence of this decision, allowing SCS time to decide how to deal with the court's ruling.
facts.F4: In 1996, the Circular was issued, constituting a new approach to the question of overseas officers transferring to pensionable terms.
facts.F5: The five-year rule, which has been in operation since April 1992, requires that an officer must have at least five years of service on pensionable terms before they can retire and claim a pension lump sum.
facts.F6: The third category of overseas officers does not stand in a similar position to those in the other two categories because they were not yet on LMT and therefore could not transfer to pensionable terms under the current rules.
facts.F7: SCS did not act unlawfully in relying on the five-year rule in this case.
facts.F8: Overseas officers who were not eligible for pensionable terms either because they were not yet on LMT or because they had reached the age of 55 before transferring from OAT to LMT are not necessitating rescue by SCS.

reference_issues: Whether the decisions made by SCS regarding the transfer of overseas officers to pensionable terms were unlawful
Whether the five-year rule is discretionary and whether it applies to overseas officers who reached their 55th birthday before becoming LMT officers

parties: Plaintiff: SHUI ON CREDIT COMPANY LIMITED

facts.F1: The Taxpayer acquired a loan facility of $600 million from Mitsubishi Bank in 1988.
facts.F2: The loan was used to purchase an interest stream from Agnew under a Centre Co. Loan.
facts.F3: The Scheme involved multiple transactions among companies within the Shui On Group, ultimately resulting in the Taxpayer claiming a deduction for the amortized consideration paid to Agnew.
facts.F4: The Board of Review held that the Taxpayer had wrongly treated the deferred expenditure as deductibles, as it was of a capital nature.
facts.F5: Alternatively, the Board applied Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap.112) s.61A, finding that the Taxpayer had entered into the Scheme to obtain a tax benefit, and the Commissioner was entitled to ignore the alleged deductibles when assessing profits tax.
facts.F6: Grounds of Appeal were filed by the Taxpayer.
facts.F7: The Taxpayer's contention on the deferred expenditure was not open to the Taxpayer based on the Grounds of Appeal.
facts.F8: The Board increased the assessment for the year of assessment 1993/94.
facts.F9: The Board confirmed all other assessments appealed against.

reference_issues: Whether the Board was correct in holding that the Taxpayer's contention on the deferred expenditure was not covered by the Grounds of Appeal and was not open to the Taxpayer.
Whether the Board was correct in holding that the deferred expenditure was not deductible under sections 14, 16, and 17 of the IRO.
Whether the Board was correct in increasing the assessment for the year of assessment 1993/94 and confirming all other assessments appealed against.

Whether the Board was correct in holding that the Taxpayer and other participants in the Scheme entered into or carried out the Scheme for the dominant purpose of enabling the Taxpayer to obtain a tax benefit.

Whether the differential treatment between same-sex couples and opposite-sex couples under the Spousal Policy is rationally connected to the legitimate aim of supporting traditional family formations
